extracted.intended_audience: readers/subscribers of Popular Science Monthly; educated general public and practicing scientists interested in popular-science commentary and book reviews
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether a proposed scientific hypothesis or claim qualifies as scientific — focusing on clarity, definiteness, testability, and the quality/selection of evidence. Also covers related expectations for scientific publications and practical bulletins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner's directions for mind-reading experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief points for the beginner to observe are: 1. Impress upon your 'subject' the necessity of fixing his mind on the object and its locality. 2. Concentrate your attention on every movement of the subject. 3. Never hazard a guess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The experiments can involve half a dozen or more persons each performing parts while ignorant of others' actions; the performer unravels the thread by beginning at the end and working backward or vice versa. Experiments are rapid and sometimes take less time to perform than to arrange them. The author refers readers to a previous explanation of performances without physical contact and expresses hope these directions will enable successful repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentials of a legitimate scientific hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or three things are essential to a legitimate scientific hypothesis: It must be expressed in intelligible terms; it must present a definite subject-matter for solution or determination; and it must be one by which predictions can be made that can be proved or disproved by experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When offering a hypothesis for scientific investigation it must be stated intelligibly, define a clear subject for enquiry, and permit testable predictions. Extraordinary or controversial claims should be investigated on the same terms and conditions as other natural problems. Lack of any of these essentials renders a claim unscientific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and selection of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The admissibility and weight of evidence hinge upon its character; good scientific practice requires discrimination in selecting and weighing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include promiscuously assembling Bible stories, legends, newspaper reports, anecdotal phenomena, psychological fiction, and scientific research as if they had equal weight; failing to arrange material systematically; and offering no real reasoning or argument. Legitimate scientific claims should be supported by evidence that allows predictions to be tested experimentally; authors should exercise discrimination in what they accept as supporting data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical textbook qualities (example: organic chemistry for medical students)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical textbook intended 'with especial reference to the requirements of medical students' should be a concise and perspicuous outline of the subject, follow some previous foundational work, and be neat in form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helpful features include parenthetical references to authorities and original papers, giving due prominence to relevant (e.g., national) research, thoughtful selection (preferring a concise useful manual over a larger bewildering compendium), and being supplemented by a careful and copious index and clear presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional requirements for government scientific bulletins (entomological example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bulletins issued under a governmental survey/commission should contain special information of interest or importance connected with the commission's objects, including practical instruction and natural-history compendia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: provide clear, actionable instructions (e.g., timing for destroying young insects — April, May, June); natural history and habits of pests (locusts); useful illustrations (woodcuts) and maps; and be authored or overseen by qualified specialists (e.g., Prof. C. V. Riley). Such bulletins should be timely and practically useful to the target audience (farmers, regional authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial perspective on awarding honorary academic degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: An honorary degree may be interpreted either as recognition of important scientific services in the general field of natural history/science or as an endorsement of doctrines associated with the recipient; institutions often delay honors until fame is secured rather than detecting merit early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers/evaluators should note the dual possible readings of conferring honors (recognition of service vs. doctrinal endorsement). The editorial view expressed is that universities should be more alert to detect and honor merit early when such recognition would benefit recipients, rather than waiting until the recipient's fame yields the institution greater advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities expected in a serious critical philosophical/ethical work (Sidgwick review)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work in ethics that is critical in character should examine the grounds and sufficiency of existing methods rather than merely propound a new system; clarity of statement is important to avoid perplexity about the author's views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful revisions include explanatory and supplementary alterations to reduce intricacy and obscurity. Authors should make clearer what they themselves believe and indicate modifications in light of related theories (e.g., evolution) rather than leaving readers uncertain of the author's position.
